entries.title: Elevators, toasters, and the birth of Java
entries.summary: Ryan sits down with James Gosling, creator of Java at Sun Microsystems, to talk about the early networking friction that drove the need for interconnectedness, the stringent reliability requirements of consumer electronics companies that inspired the Java virtual machine, and the evolution of garbage collectors that allow Java to handle large-scale concurrent memory management.
entries.content:
Ryan sits down with James Gosling, creator of Java at Sun Microsystems, to talk about the early networking friction that drove the need for interconnectedness, the stringent reliability requirements of consumer electronics companies that inspired the Java virtual machine, and the evolution of garbage collectors that allow Java to handle large-scale concurrent memory management.

Check out CultRepo’s recently released Java documentary to learn more about the early history of the language and the engineers who built it.

entries.title: Rumors of the SaaS demise are greatly exaggerated
entries.summary: Recorded on the floor of LDX3, Ryan chats with Nivia Henry, an engineering leader most recently at Netflix, about the reality of the supposed SaaS apocalypse, the complex calculus of the modern build-versus-buy decision in the era of AI, and the critical importance of understanding system architectures to manage long-term infrastructure costs.
entries.content:
Recorded on the floor of LDX3, Ryan chats with Nivia Henry, an engineering leader most recently at Netflix, about the reality of the supposed SaaS apocalypse, the complex calculus of the modern build-versus-buy decision in the era of AI, and the critical importance of understanding system architectures to manage long-term infrastructure costs.

This episode was recorded at this year’s LDX3 by LeadDev, a conference focused on modern engineering leadership, management, and technical strategy

Nivia recently spent two and a half years tackling complex data and engineering challenges at Netflix and previously spent eight years driving product innovation at Spotify.

entries.title: The Regression Tests Nobody Writes: Capturing How Software Actually Behaves
entries.content:
Here’s an awkward question for any codebase that’s been around a few years. Do your tests describe what the system does? Or what somebody, at some point, thought it should do?

Not the same thing. Not even close, usually. Most regression tests get written right alongside a feature, by people writing down their intentions. This function returns that. This endpoint rejects bad input. Perfectly good tests! But give a system a few years in production and it picks up a whole extra layer of behavior that nobody planned and nobody wrote down. Quirks. Weird edge cases. A default value someone picked in 2019 for reasons that are now completely lost. And I’d bet money some of your users, or some other team’s service, quietly depends on every one of them.

That’s where a lot of the really nasty regressions live. And funnily enough, there’s a kind of test built for exactly that gap. Almost nobody writes it.

Hyrum’s Law and the behavior nobody documented

You’ve probably heard of Hyrum’s Law, named after Hyrum Wright at Google. The gist: once enough people use your API, every observable behavior of your system ends up being depended on by somebody. Not just the documented contract. All of it. The order results come back in. The exact wording of an error. How long a call takes. Whether an empty field shows up as null or just... doesn’t show up.

If you’ve ever maintained something popular, you’ve lived this. You fix a thing that was obviously wrong, ship it, feel good about yourself, and within the hour there’s a bug report from someone whose integration was built on the wrong thing. To them, you just broke their stuff. And are they wrong? Not really.

Regular regression tests can’t help much here. They only check what somebody thought to check. Everything accidental slips right through.

What characterization tests actually are

Michael Feathers put a name on this back in Working Effectively with Legacy Code. He called them characterization tests, and the idea is almost cheeky. Before you touch code you don’t fully understand, you write tests that capture what it does right now. Not what it should do. What it actually does.

Run the code, see what comes out, pin that in a test. Looks like a bug? Pin it anyway, maybe leave yourself a note. Correctness isn’t the goal here. The goal is a safety net that yells the moment behavior shifts.

It’s kind of a mental flip, honestly. A normal test says “here’s what I want, code, please live up to it.” A characterization test says “here’s what’s real, and if you change it, you’d better have a reason.”

Why almost nobody writes them

So if they’re that useful, why doesn’t everyone have a pile of them? Mostly human reasons.

They’re a slog to write. Characterizing one gnarly function means throwing a bunch of inputs at it and carefully noting every output. Characterizing a whole service? Now you’re doing that across every endpoint, every odd case, every conversation it has with some downstream system. Who’s got time for that?

They also just feel wrong. Writing a test that asserts behavior you’re pretty sure is a bug goes against every instinct a developer’s got. It takes a real shift to see that pinning the bug is the whole point. You’re not saying it’s fine. You’re making sure that if it ever changes, someone decided to change it.

Golden masters and snapshot tests

People have been chipping away at the slog for years. Golden master testing, which some folks call approval testing, grabs a big chunk of output once, saves it as the blessed version, and checks every future run against it. Frontend snapshot tests run on the same instinct. Both make characterization way cheaper, since you’re capturing output all at once instead of asserting on it one field at a time.

Where they really shine is stuff you can call directly. A function. A report generator. A rendered component. Services are trickier, though. A service’s behavior isn’t just what it returns. It’s how it reacts to real requests, and everything it does along the way. Which queries it runs. Which other services it calls. Which messages it fires off.

Characterizing a whole service with real traffic

And this is where it gets fun if you run services in production. The best record of how your service actually behaves isn’t sitting in a test file anywhere. It’s in the traffic.

Think about it. Every real request and response is basically a characterization test that hasn’t been written yet. Capture what comes into a service and what goes back out, and you’ve pinned how it behaves for real inputs, including all the strange ones nobody would ever dream up by hand. Capture what it sends to its own dependencies too, and now you’ve got its side effects pinned as well.

Recording down at the network level makes this doable without touching the application code, and it catches database and queue traffic right along with HTTP. Replay those recordings later, with dependencies answered from that same capture, and you’ve got a characterization suite that behaves the same way every run. Same inputs in, same downstream behavior. If a response changes, or the service suddenly makes an extra database call, it shows up in the diff.

That last bit doesn’t get enough credit. Some of the most expensive regressions keep the response exactly the same while quietly changing what happens underneath. A new query that’s harmless in testing and brutal at scale, say. A suite built on real traffic catches those too.

Living with characterization tests

They fail differently than normal tests, and that takes a bit of getting used to.

A red characterization test doesn’t mean “bug.” It means “behavior changed.” And the very next question is always, did we mean that? Sometimes yes. You fixed the quirk on purpose, you warned the folks relying on it, and the new behavior becomes the new baseline. Sometimes no, and congrats, you just caught a regression no intent-based test was ever going to notice.

Either way you’re better off than finding out from a user. Teams that review these diffs in pull requests tend to pick up a really healthy habit: behavior changes stop being accidents and start being decisions. The diff turns into a little conversation. Did we actually want this?

Noise needs some attention, though. Timestamps and generated IDs change every run, and they’ll drown out the real signal if you let them. Ignore those specific fields, and nothing broader, and the suite stays honest.

Where this pays off most

A handful of situations keep coming up where these tests really earn their keep.

Refactoring legacy code is the classic one, the case Feathers was writing about in the first place. Pin the behavior, then move things around without the cold sweat.

Framework and library upgrades are another. A new major version of your web framework or ORM can nudge behavior in tiny ways intent-based tests never look at, like how something serializes or what order results come back in.

Rewrites might be the best case of all. When a team ports a service to a new language or a new architecture, the old service’s recorded traffic basically becomes the spec for the new one. Fire the same requests at both. Any difference is either a deliberate improvement or a regression. No more arguing about what the old system was “supposed” to do.

And then there’s AI-assisted changes, which are only getting more common. When an assistant drafts a big refactor and updates the tests in the same go, a baseline captured beforehand is one of the very few checks that doesn’t share the same assumptions as the change itself.

Conclusion

Here’s how I’ve come to see it. Every long-lived codebase has two specs. One lives in its tests. The other lives in its behavior. Most regression testing only protects the first, and for any system with real users, the second one is often the one that bites.

Want to try it? Pick a service you’re a little scared to change. Before your next refactor, capture what it really does, run your change against that baseline, and look hard at every difference. I’d bet you find at least one behavior you didn’t know you had. Much nicer to meet it in a diff than in a bug report.

entries.title: Building Immersive Virtual Economies: An Introduction to KursarScript (KSPL)
entries.content:
As developers, we are constantly exploring how software intersects with evolving digital frontiers like virtual reality (VR) and immersive ecosystems. Recently, I’ve been diving into KursarScript Programming Language (KSPL)—a specialized programming language designed specifically for managing virtual environments, digital currencies, and interactive virtual economies.

In this article, we’ll take a look at what makes KursarScript unique, how it handles virtual assets, and how we can model its concepts using Python.

What is KursarScript?

  • KursarScript (KSPL) is a user-friendly programming language tailored for virtual realities.
  • Rather than focusing solely on traditional backend or web logic, KSPL is built to manage digital currencies, virtual assets, and real-time financial transactions via interactive denominators like coins and banknotes.
  • A standout ecosystem concept in KSPL is the Virtu-Card, a digital system that enables users to securely store, tap, and transfer virtual funds.
  • Businesses can leverage Virtual-Terminals—service hubs embedded into websites within a VR environment—allowing avatars to buy and sell products or services across interconnected marketplaces known as Virtual Portals.

Core Features and Architecture

1. Object-Oriented Design (Without Inheritance)

  • KSPL follows an object-oriented programming (OOP) paradigm to help model real-world elements and reusable code structures.
  • No Inheritance or Polymorphism: To keep object management simple within immersive landscapes, KSPL deliberately excludes support for inheritance and polymorphism.
  • Avatars as Active Participants: Avatars act as active participants inside the VR environment, capable of instantiating classes, interacting with objects, and executing transactions.

2. AI-Inspired Concepts

  • While not strictly an AI programming language, KSPL incorporates artificial intelligence principles to enable smart, automated operations.
  • This includes seamless integration with AI-based modules for automated currency exchanges and smart contract execution within virtual worlds.

Code in Action: KursarScript Concepts in Python

To see how these object-oriented and virtual economic concepts operate in practice, let's translate the core KSPL examples into equivalent Python code structures:

Defining and Using Virtual Items

Object creation in KSPL uses familiar class structures. Defining a 

VirtualItem
with a name and price translates to Python like this:

Python 
      
class VirtualItem:
    def __init__(self, name: str, price: float):
        self.name = name
        self.price = price
        
    def display_item(self):
        print(f"Item: {self.name} Price: {self.price}")

Instantiating and displaying that item in your virtual world can be written in Python as:

Python

      
item1 = VirtualItem("Digital Sword", 120.99)
item1.display_item()

Managing Virtual Economies with Virtu-Cards

Handling currency through a 

Virtu-Card
involves tapping denominators (like coins or banknotes) to update balances in real time:

Python 
      
class VirtuCard:
    def __init__(self):
        self.balance = 0.0
        
    def tap_denominator(self, amount: float):
        self.balance += amount
        print(f"Added {amount} to Virtu-Card. New balance: {self.balance}")

my_card = VirtuCard()
my_card.tap_denominator(50.0)

Performing Transactions via Virtual-Terminals

Avatars can interact with business service hubs to execute purchases against their card balances:

Python

      
class VirtualTerminal:
    def perform_transaction(self, card: VirtuCard, amount: float):
        if card.balance >= amount:
            card.balance -= amount
            print(f"Transaction of {amount} completed. Remaining balance: {card.balance}")
        else:
            print("Insufficient funds.")

terminal = VirtualTerminal()
terminal.perform_transaction(my_card, 20.0)

Final Thoughts

As virtual reality and simulated economies continue to grow, languages and design patterns like those found in KursarScript offer a fascinating glimpse into how we might structure commerce, asset management, and avatar interactions in three-dimensional spaces. By tailoring data types, object structures, and transaction models specifically for virtual environments, KSPL provides a compelling blueprint for developers building the next wave of digital marketplaces.

entries.title: Survey Says: You'll swap the model, but everything you build around it is staying put
entries.summary: Earlier this month, my team at Stacklok surveyed 520 technical leaders to understand whether they were concerned about being locked into frontier labs. The data says they’re already swapping models in and out, but the trap they’re concerned about is the layer on top of the model.
entries.content:
[Ed. note: We’re big fans of data that supports some of the stories we’re hearing around the industry. We’ve been hearing plenty of conflicting information about the value of a harness vs. a model. The folks at Stacklok did some research on agents offered to share their survey results with our community and give a little context on what it all means.]

As a co-creator of Kubernetes, I spent a good chunk of my career working to protect enterprises from being trapped by infrastructure. Kubernetes has thrived over the past decade in part because enterprises want to pick their vendors, not belong to them. Does that sentiment persist as we move into the AI-native era?

Earlier this month, my team at Stacklok surveyed 520 technical leaders to understand whether they were concerned about being locked into frontier labs. The data says they’re already swapping models in and out, but the trap they’re concerned about is the layer on top of the model.

A note on our sample. Every respondent runs LLMs or agents in pilot or production at a North American company with more than 500 employees and holds a manager-or-above title.

Nobody is single-model anymore

Only 8% of respondent organizations use one model provider, whereas 25% use five or more. It’s already a multi-model world in the enterprise. Lock-in at the model layer appears to be a solved problem.

So what's hard to move? The integrations. Fifty-three percent of respondents named "integrations to internal systems or MCP servers" as one of their two hardest elements to migrate. Multi-step agent workflows are right behind at 52%. Guardrails and access-control config come next. And if you move to another model provider, these integrations don’t move with you; they have to be re-built.

Lock-in is a concern, but not a buying criteria

Eighty-one percent of these leaders agree that frontier labs and hyperscalers make it hard to move between vendors. Eighty-four percent say avoiding lock-in is important to their AI strategy. More than 80% of respondent organizations have already delayed, scaled back, or restructured a migration because switching costs looked too high; 29% say it happens frequently. And when asked how long a migration off their current provider would take, 57% said four months or more.

But as someone who thinks a lot about preserving optionality and avoiding lock-in, here’s the part that stings. When asked what actually factors into AI, "Ability to switch model providers without rebuilding" ranked sixth out of eight possible criteria. "Avoiding dependence on a single vendor" ranked dead last.

The ranking is rational, and that’s what stings. Security and privacy are the priorities, followed by cost control and compliance. The person choosing the stack today gets judged on this quarter’s bill and this year’s audit, not on a rebuild two years from now; migrations between models and providers is a problem for later (and possibly for a future team).

The people running five models have figured something out

Here’s where the organizations using five or more model providers look different from everyone else…they are building optionality into their AI architecture now.

Let’s compare organizations with five or more model providers to those with just one or two model providers. Seventy-six percent of the former have built integrations to internal systems or MCP servers, versus 42% of the latter. Forty-five percent use open source agent frameworks, versus 22%. Sixty-seven percent say portability across providers is critically or very important, compared to 47%. And 35% say they're "highly likely" to evaluate an open source alternative to the vertically integrated stacks from frontier labs, versus 13%.

If your organization is using five or more model providers or will be in the future, it’s time to think about flexibility. Once you run enough heterogeneous things, you stop tolerating a harness that only works with one of them, and you start treating the model the way we eventually learned to treat the node: as a replaceable component behind a stable interface. The teams furthest along didn't get there through principle. They got there because running five providers through five bespoke integration layers is miserable.

What respondents want from an open architecture

The appetite for a more open alternative is broad. Eighty percent say they'd be likely to evaluate an open alternative to closed frontier architectures, and 88% expect to take more control of their AI architecture as they gain experience rather than continuing to lean on current vendors.

They're also specific about the concerns keeping them up at night when building on a closed platform. Thirty-nine percent of respondents mentioned product or API deprecation, and 37% worry specifically about being unable to export agent state, memory, or evals. People are starting to see their agent layer as an asset that can be held hostage.

When we asked what would get them to move more workloads to an open architecture, the answers were practical rather than ideological. Security and compliance guarantees, performance parity with frontier models, and an enterprise support model. They want to keep the frontier models they already use and get an open harness with comparable features.

What to do next

If you're writing MCP servers, agent workflows, or policy config today, you are building the layer this survey says is hardest to move. A few things are worth doing while it's still cheap.

Keep tool definitions on the open protocol rather than a vendor's extension of it. Put orchestration in code you own. Make sure your evals can run against any model endpoint. Build (don’t rent) a harness that keeps you in control of identity, memory, tools, and more. And finally, find experts that you trust to help you navigate this fast-changing landscape.

The full report is free (no forms) and includes additional data and detail.
